claim: The ~30 cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases are characterized by the presence of a tyrosine kinase domain and one or more modular binding domains, such as SH2 and SH3 domains.
source: The ~30 cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases are characterized by the presence of a tyrosine kinase domain and one or more modular binding domains, such as SH2 and SH3 domains (Robinson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robinson et al., 2000, which provides established knowledge about tyrosine kinase structure.

claim: The catalytic activities of the tyrosine kinase domains are weak.
source: The catalytic activities of the tyrosine kinase domains are weak and, as a consequence, the binding domains strongly influence specificity by localizing the kinases to the vicinity of phosphorylation targets (Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller, 2003.

claim: The binding domains strongly influence specificity by localizing the kinases to the vicinity of phosphorylation targets.
source: The catalytic activities of the tyrosine kinase domains are weak and, as a consequence, the binding domains strongly influence specificity by localizing the kinases to the vicinity of phosphorylation targets (Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller, 2003.

claim: The individual catalytic domains of tyrosine kinases display some intrinsic preference for sequence features surrounding the phosphorylated tyrosine residues in their substrates.
source: The individual catalytic domains of tyrosine kinases display some intrinsic preference for sequence features surrounding the phosphorylated tyrosine residues in their substrates (Songyang et al., 1995), but the current understanding of tyrosine kinase mechanism emphasizes localization by the modular binding domains as a principal mechanism for gaining specificity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Songyang et al., 1995.

claim: There is an important role for direct substrate selection by the kinase active sites of Lck and ZAP-70 in the response of T cells to antigen recognition.
source: We have shown recently that there is an important role for direct substrate selection by the kinase active sites of two cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases, the Src-family kinase Lck and the Syk-family kinase ZAP-70, in the response of T cells to antigen recognition (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2016, which is a previous study by the authors.

claim: T cell activation requires the sequential action of Lck and ZAP-70.
source: T cell activation requires the sequential action of Lck and ZAP-70 (Figure 1A) (Iwashima et al., 1994; Weiss and Littman, 1994; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iwashima et al., 1994; Weiss and Littman, 1994; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014, and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Lck phosphorylates the ITAM motifs of the T cell antigen receptor, creating binding sites for ZAP-70.
source: First, Lck phosphorylates the ITAM motifs of the T cell antigen receptor, creating binding sites for ZAP-70, and Lck then phosphorylates ZAP-70 and releases its autoinhibition.
evidence: This claim is part of the description of the T cell activation pathway and is supported by the context of the cited literature.

claim: Lck phosphorylates ZAP-70 and releases its autoinhibition.
source: First, Lck phosphorylates the ITAM motifs of the T cell antigen receptor, creating binding sites for ZAP-70, and Lck then phosphorylates ZAP-70 and releases its autoinhibition.
evidence: This claim is part of the description of the T cell activation pathway and is supported by the context of the cited literature.

claim: Once recruited to the T cell receptor and activated by Lck, ZAP-70 phosphorylates the scaffold proteins LAT and SLP-76.
source: Once recruited to the T cell receptor and activated by Lck, ZAP-70 phosphorylates the scaffold proteins LAT and SLP-76, leading to the recruitment of other signaling proteins, such as phospholipase Cγ1 and the Ras activator SOS via the adapter protein Grb2.
evidence: This claim is part of the description of the T cell activation pathway and is supported by the context of the cited literature.

claim: ZAP-70 phosphorylation of LAT and SLP-76 leads to the recruitment of other signaling proteins, such as phospholipase Cγ1 and the Ras activator SOS via the adapter protein Grb2.
source: Once recruited to the T cell receptor and activated by Lck, ZAP-70 phosphorylates the scaffold proteins LAT and SLP-76, leading to the recruitment of other signaling proteins, such as phospholipase Cγ1 and the Ras activator SOS via the adapter protein Grb2.
evidence: This claim is part of the description of the T cell activation pathway and is supported by the context of the cited literature.

claim: The strictly sequential action of Lck and ZAP-70 reflects the inability of the kinase domain of Lck to phosphorylate LAT and SLP-76 efficiently.
source: The strictly sequential action of Lck and ZAP-70 reflects the inability of the kinase domain of Lck to phosphorylate LAT and SLP-76 efficiently, and the inability of ZAP-70 to phosphorylate ITAMs and to activate itself.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work and the logic of the T cell signaling pathway.

claim: ZAP-70 is unable to phosphorylate ITAMs and to activate itself.
source: The strictly sequential action of Lck and ZAP-70 reflects the inability of the kinase domain of Lck to phosphorylate LAT and SLP-76 efficiently, and the inability of ZAP-70 to phosphorylate ITAMs and to activate itself.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work and the logic of the T cell signaling pathway.

claim: The orthogonality in the specificities of the kinase domains of Lck and ZAP-70, combined with the targeting functions of their binding domains, is postulated to underlie the sensitivity and selectivity of the T cell response to antigens.
source: This orthogonality in the specificities of the kinase domains of Lck and ZAP-70, combined with the targeting functions of their binding domains, is postulated to underlie the sensitivity and selectivity of the T cell response to antigens.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the authors' previous work and the understanding of T cell signaling.

claim: A high-throughput platform was adapted to simultaneously measure the efficiency of phosphorylation by a tyrosine kinase of hundreds of genetically encoded peptides in bacterial surface-display libraries.
source: To analyze the differential specificities of Lck and ZAP-70, we had adapted a high-throughput platform to simultaneously measure the efficiency of phosphorylation by a tyrosine kinase of hundreds of genetically encoded peptides in bacterial surface-display libraries (Figure 1B) (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2016 and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Peptides are expressed on the extracellular surface of bacterial cells as fusions to a scaffold protein, with one peptide of defined sequence per cell.
source: In this method, peptides are expressed on the extracellular surface of bacterial cells as fusions to a scaffold protein, with one peptide of defined sequence per cell (Rice and Daugherty, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rice and Daugherty, 2008.

claim: Addition of a purified kinase to the cell suspension results in phosphorylation of the displayed peptides.
source: Addition of a purified kinase to the cell suspension results in phosphorylation of the displayed peptides (Henriques et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Henriques et al., 2013.

claim: Deep sequencing of the peptide-coding DNA before and after sorting yields a quantitative metric of the efficiency with which each substrate is phosphorylated by the kinase, the 'enrichment score'.
source: Deep sequencing of the peptide-coding DNA before and after sorting yields a quantitative metric of the efficiency with which each substrate is phosphorylated by the kinase, the 'enrichment score' (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2016.

claim: The enrichment score correlates strongly with the rate of phosphorylation measured in vitro using purified peptides and kinases.
source: The enrichment score correlates strongly with the rate of phosphorylation measured in vitro using purified peptides and kinases.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous validation work.

claim: ZAP-70 and Lck differentiate their respective substrates on the basis of an electrostatic-selection mechanism that is encoded within their kinase domains.
source: This analysis showed that ZAP-70 and Lck differentiate their respective substrates on the basis of an electrostatic-selection mechanism that is encoded within their kinase domains.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous analysis using scanning-mutagenesis libraries.

claim: The phosphosites in LAT are flanked by many negatively charged residues, and this increases the efficiency of phosphorylation by ZAP-70 and reduces that by Lck.
source: The phosphosites in LAT are flanked by many negatively charged residues, and this increases the efficiency of phosphorylation by ZAP-70 and reduces that by Lck.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous analysis using scanning-mutagenesis libraries.

claim: The ITAM motifs on the T cell receptor bear positively-charged residues that deter phosphorylation by ZAP-70, but promote phosphorylation by Lck.
source: By contrast, the ITAM motifs on the T cell receptor bear positively-charged residues that deter phosphorylation by ZAP-70, but promote phosphorylation by Lck.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous analysis using scanning-mutagenesis libraries.

claim: Lck is one of eight Src-family kinases in the human genome.
source: Lck is one of eight Src-family kinases in the human genome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is established knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The Src-family kinases emerged at the very root of the metazoan evolutionary tree, with a clearly identifiable Src-family kinase present in the genomes of choanoflagellates.
source: This family of kinases emerged at the very root of the metazoan evolutionary tree, with a clearly identifiable Src-family kinase present in the genomes of choanoflagellates, the closest identified relatives of the true metazoans (Richter and King, 2013), and in even more distantly related taxa (Suga et al., 2012; Suga et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Richter and King, 2013; Suga et al., 2012; Suga et al., 2014.

claim: In humans, the Src-family kinases fall into two groups, the Src-A and Src-B subfamilies.
source: In humans, the Src-family kinases fall into two groups, the Src-A and Src-B subfamilies (Hughes, 1996; Suga et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hughes, 1996; Suga et al., 1997.

claim: The Src-A kinases, which include c-Src, are expressed in a wide variety of cell types.
source: The Src-A kinases, which include the extremely well studied kinase c-Src, are expressed in a wide variety of cell types.
evidence: This claim is established knowledge about Src-A kinases.

claim: Lck and other Src-B kinases are restricted to cells from the hematopoietic lineage, such as T cells and B cells.
source: In contrast, Lck and other Src-B kinases are restricted to cells from the hematopoietic lineage, such as T cells and B cells (Lowell and Soriano, 1996; Thomas and Brugge, 1997; Bolen and Brugge, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lowell and Soriano, 1996; Thomas and Brugge, 1997; Bolen and Brugge, 1997.

claim: Each of the Src-family kinases are closely related in sequence, with 64–90% sequence identity in their catalytic domains.
source: Except for unique N-terminal segments that include membrane-localization motifs (Resh, 1994), each of the Src-family kinases are closely related in sequence, with 64–90% sequence identity in their catalytic domains, and have very similar three-dimensional structures (Sicheri et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1997; Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996; Williams et al., 1997; Boggon and Eck, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Resh, 1994; Sicheri et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1997; Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996; Williams et al., 1997; Boggon and Eck, 2004.

claim: Src-family kinases have very similar three-dimensional structures.
source: Except for unique N-terminal segments that include membrane-localization motifs (Resh, 1994), each of the Src-family kinases are closely related in sequence, with 64–90% sequence identity in their catalytic domains, and have very similar three-dimensional structures (Sicheri et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1997; Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996; Williams et al., 1997; Boggon and Eck, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sicheri et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1997; Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996; Williams et al., 1997; Boggon and Eck, 2004.

claim: All eight of the human Src-family kinases have similar substrate sequence preferences.
source: Prior studies employing peptide library screens with degenerate sequences have shown that all eight of the human Src-family kinases have similar substrate sequence preferences (Songyang et al., 1995; Schmitz et al., 1996; Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Songyang et al., 1995; Schmitz et al., 1996; Deng et al., 2014.

claim: Src-family kinases prefer a large aliphatic residue immediately upstream of the target tyrosine residue in their substrates.
source: For example, they prefer a large aliphatic residue immediately upstream of the target tyrosine residue in their substrates, a feature that distinguishes their specificity from that of ZAP-70, which prefers an aspartic acid residue at this position (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2016.

claim: ZAP-70 prefers an aspartic acid residue at the -1 position relative to the target tyrosine.
source: For example, they prefer a large aliphatic residue immediately upstream of the target tyrosine residue in their substrates, a feature that distinguishes their specificity from that of ZAP-70, which prefers an aspartic acid residue at this position (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2016.

claim: A genetically encoded peptide library containing ~2600 diverse sequences derived from known tyrosine phosphorylation sites in the human proteome was constructed.
source: We have now expanded our kinase specificity screening platform through construction of a genetically encoded peptide library containing ~2600 diverse sequences derived from known tyrosine phosphorylation sites in the human proteome.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental work performed in this study.

claim: Using the Human-pTyr library, the earlier conclusions regarding the orthogonal specificities of Lck and ZAP-70 were validated.
source: Using this library, we validated our earlier conclusions regarding the orthogonal specificities of Lck and ZAP-70.
evidence: This claim describes the results of the experiments performed in this study.

claim: There is a subtle, but significant, divergence in the substrate preferences of Lck and c-Src.
source: In comparing the specificity of Lck to that of c-Src using this library, we find a subtle, but significant, divergence in the substrate preferences of these two enzymes.
evidence: This claim describes the results of the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Both Lck and c-Src are equally efficient at phosphorylating a large group of common substrates.
source: While both Src-family kinases are equally efficient at phosphorylating a large group of common substrates, there are peptides that are phosphorylated efficiently by c-Src and not by Lck, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim describes the results of the experiments performed in this study.

claim: There are peptides that are phosphorylated efficiently by c-Src and not by Lck, and vice versa.
source: While both Src-family kinases are equally efficient at phosphorylating a large group of common substrates, there are peptides that are phosphorylated efficiently by c-Src and not by Lck, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim describes the results of the experiments performed in this study.

claim: The divergence between Lck and c-Src is characterized by a suppression in the ability of Lck, relative to c-Src, to phosphorylate highly acidic phosphosites while tolerating the presence of positively charged residues in the substrates.
source: This divergence is characterized by a suppression in the ability of Lck, relative to c-Src, to phosphorylate highly acidic phosphosites while tolerating the presence of positively charged residues in the substrates.
evidence: This claim describes the results of the experiments performed in this study.

claim: The distribution of enrichment scores for phosphorylation by the c-Abl kinase domain is bimodal, with ~70% of the peptides being poorly phosphorylated and 30% of the peptides being phosphorylated relatively efficiently.
source: The distribution of enrichment scores for phosphorylation by the c-Abl kinase domain is bimodal, with ~70% of the peptides being poorly phosphorylated and 30% of the peptides being phosphorylated relatively efficiently (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Approximately a third of the peptides in the Human-pTyr library are phosphorylated efficiently by c-Abl, which is consistent with the view that tyrosine kinases are, in general, promiscuous enzymes.
source: The fact that approximately a third of the peptides are phosphorylated efficiently is consistent with the view that tyrosine kinases are, in general, promiscuous enzymes, with the ability to target a broad range of potential substrates (Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the c-Abl screen and a citation to Miller, 2003.

claim: c-Abl has a strong preference for a bulky aliphatic residue at the −1 position with respect to the tyrosine, an alanine at the +1 position, and a proline at the +3 position.
source: Previous studies have defined three strong determinants of efficient phosphorylation by the c-Abl kinase domain: a bulky aliphatic residue at the −1 position with respect to the tyrosine, an alanine at the +1 position, and a proline at the +3 position (Songyang et al., 1995; Till et al., 1994; Till et al., 1999; Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Songyang et al., 1995; Till et al., 1994; Till et al., 1999; Deng et al., 2014.

claim: The c-Abl phospho-pLogo for the Human-pTyr library recapitulates the known sequence preferences for c-Abl.
source: The c-Abl phospho-pLogo for the Human-pTyr library recapitulates these known sequence preferences for c-Abl (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: c-Abl disfavors a proline residue at the +1 position in the substrate.
source: Our analysis also provides information about sequence features that are disfavored, such as a proline residue at the +1 position in the substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the c-Abl phospho-pLogo diagram.

claim: The distribution of enrichment scores for ZAP-70 is bimodal, with only ~20% of the peptides falling in the efficiently phosphorylated group.
source: As for c-Abl, the distribution of enrichment scores is bimodal, although the separation between the inefficient and efficient substrates is more marked, with only ~20% of the peptides falling in the latter group (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The phospho-pLogo diagram for ZAP-70 reveals a strong preference for substrates enriched in aspartate and glutamate residues, with lysine or arginine residues being disfavored.
source: As expected based on our earlier studies, the phospho-pLogo diagram for ZAP-70 reveals a strong preference for substrates enriched in aspartate and glutamate residues, with lysine or arginine residues being disfavored (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The sequence features characteristic of ZAP-70 substrates are found not just in phosphosites in LAT and SLP-76, but also in other scaffold and adapter proteins in lymphocytes, such as NTAL and LAX.
source: Interestingly, these sequence features are characteristic not just of phosphosites in LAT and SLP-76, but also those in other scaffold and adapter proteins in lymphocytes, such as NTAL and LAX.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the ZAP-70 phospho-pLogo diagram.

claim: NTAL and LAX are known substrates of the ZAP-70 paralog Syk.
source: These proteins are known substrates of the ZAP-70 paralog Syk (Horejsí et al., 2004), and are robustly phosphorylated by ZAP-70 in our screen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Horejsí et al., 2004 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: NTAL and LAX are robustly phosphorylated by ZAP-70 in the screen.
source: These proteins are known substrates of the ZAP-70 paralog Syk (Horejsí et al., 2004), and are robustly phosphorylated by ZAP-70 in our screen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phospho-pLogo diagrams generated using the most efficiently phosphorylated peptides are strikingly similar for Lck and c-Src.
source: The phospho-pLogo diagrams generated using the most efficiently phosphorylated peptides are strikingly similar for Lck and c-Src, and these logos are different from those for c-Abl and ZAP-70.
evidence: This claim is based on visual comparison of the phospho-pLogo diagrams.

claim: The phospho-pLogo diagrams for Lck and c-Src are different from those for c-Abl and ZAP-70.
source: The phospho-pLogo diagrams generated using the most efficiently phosphorylated peptides are strikingly similar for Lck and c-Src, and these logos are different from those for c-Abl and ZAP-70.
evidence: This claim is based on visual comparison of the phospho-pLogo diagrams.

claim: The observed substrate preferences for Lck and c-Src are in line with preferences observed previously using oriented peptide libraries composed of degenerate sequences.
source: The observed substrate preferences for Lck and c-Src are in line with preferences observed previously using oriented peptide libraries composed of degenerate sequences (Figure 2E–F) (Songyang et al., 1995; Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Songyang et al., 1995; Deng et al., 2014 and data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Both Lck and c-Src have a strong preference for isoleucine, leucine, or valine at the −1 position.
source: Both kinases had a strong preference for isoleucine, leucine, or valine at the −1 position, and a moderate preference for a bulky hydrophobic residue at the +3 position.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the phospho-pLogo diagrams for Lck and c-Src.

claim: Both Lck and c-Src have a moderate preference for a bulky hydrophobic residue at the +3 position.
source: Both kinases had a strong preference for isoleucine, leucine, or valine at the −1 position, and a moderate preference for a bulky hydrophobic residue at the +3 position.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the phospho-pLogo diagrams for Lck and c-Src.

claim: A subtle distinction between Lck and c-Src emerges upon comparing the efficiency of phosphorylation of individual peptides by different kinases.
source: A subtle distinction between Lck and c-Src emerges, however, upon comparing the efficiency of phosphorylation of individual peptides by different kinases (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Comparison of duplicate experiments with Lck shows a high degree of correlation in the efficiency of phosphorylation for each peptide in the Human-pTyr library.
source: Comparison of duplicate experiments with Lck shows a high degree of correlation in the efficiency of phosphorylation for each peptide in the Human-pTyr library (Figure 3A, first panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, first panel.

claim: On comparing Lck and c-Src, there is still a high degree of correlation between the two datasets, with 26 and 65% of the peptides being good or bad substrates, respectively, for both kinases.
source: On comparing Lck and c-Src, a difference is evident (Figure 3A, second panel). Although there is still a high degree of correlation between the two datasets, with 26 and 65% of the peptides being good or bad substrates, respectively, for both kinases, ~10% of the substrates were only phosphorylated efficiently by one kinase but not the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, second panel.

claim: ~10% of the substrates in the Human-pTyr library were only phosphorylated efficiently by one kinase (Lck or c-Src) but not the other.
source: On comparing Lck and c-Src, a difference is evident (Figure 3A, second panel). Although there is still a high degree of correlation between the two datasets, with 26 and 65% of the peptides being good or bad substrates, respectively, for both kinases, ~10% of the substrates were only phosphorylated efficiently by one kinase but not the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, second panel.

claim: When comparing phosphorylation by Lck to that by c-Abl and ZAP-70, the exclusion effect is much stronger.
source: When comparing phosphorylation by Lck to that by c-Abl and ZAP-70, the exclusion effect is much stronger, with an orthogonality in specificity most clearly demonstrated for the comparison of Lck and ZAP-70 (Figure 3A, third and fourth panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, third and fourth panels.

claim: For the c-Src-preferred peptides, there is an over-representation of negatively charged residues C-terminal to the phosphotyrosine, and an under-representation of positively charged residues.
source: For the c-Src-preferred peptides, there is an over-representation of negatively charged residues C-terminal to the phosphotyrosine, and an under-representation of positively charged residues (Figure 3B, top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, top panel.

claim: For the Lck-preferred peptides, there is an under-representation of negatively charged residues C-terminal to the phosphotyrosine, and an over-representation of positively charged residues.
source: The opposite is true for the Lck-preferred peptides (Figure 3B, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, bottom panel.

claim: c-Src is more tolerant of negatively charged residues in substrates than Lck, and less tolerant of positively charged residues.
source: Our results indicate that c-Src is more tolerant of negatively charged residues in substrates than Lck, and less tolerant of positively charged residues.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the phospho-pLogo diagrams and differential enrichment scores.

claim: The sharp differential selectivity for charged residues between ZAP-70 and Lck is also seen, in muted form, between c-Src and Lck.
source: In Figure 3C, we show the differential enrichment scores for phosphorylation of all sequences in the Human-pTyr library by c-Src versus Lck, and by ZAP-70 versus Lck, focusing on Asp, Glu, Arg and Lys residues at each position along the peptide. The sharp differential selectivity for charged residues between ZAP-70 and Lck is also seen, in muted form, between c-Src and Lck.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The peptides favored by c-Src have significantly greater net negative charge than those favored by Lck.
source: The peptides favored by c-Src have significantly greater net negative charge than those favored by Lck, pointing to an electrostatic basis for the differential specificity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In vitro measurements of phosphorylation kinetics with purified kinase domains and five representative synthetic peptides are consistent with the screening data.
source: Consistent with our screens, the c-Src-preferred peptides were readily phosphorylated by c-Src but not by Lck, both Lck-preferred peptides were phosphorylated efficiently by Lck, but with either reduced or negligible efficiency by c-Src, and the predicted common substrate was phosphorylated robustly by both kinases (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lck has presumably evolved to suppress off-target phosphorylation of the highly negatively charged ZAP-70 substrates in T cells, LAT and SLP-76.
source: Lck has presumably evolved to suppress off-target phosphorylation of the highly negatively charged ZAP-70 substrates in T cells, LAT and SLP-76.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the observed specificity differences.

claim: This electrostatic fine-tuning may be a conserved feature that differentiates the Src-A and Src-B lineages.
source: Given that similar substrates exist in other hematopoietic cell types, where signaling also requires an interplay between Src- and Syk-family kinases (Weiss and Littman, 1994; Lowell, 2011), this electrostatic fine-tuning may be a conserved feature that differentiates the Src-A and Src-B lineages.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the observed specificity differences and citations to Weiss and Littman, 1994; Lowell, 2011.

claim: Three positions near the substrate docking site were identified where the charge on the residue is maintained within the Src-A and Src-B families, but not between the two groups.
source: We analyzed the sequences of Src-family kinase domains across vertebrates and identified three positions near the substrate docking site where the charge on the residue is maintained within the Src-A and Src-B families, but not between the two groups (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glu 398 in Lck (Gln 423 in c-Src) lies in the activation loop and is poised to sense charged residues downstream of the substrate tyrosine.
source: One of these residues, Glu 398 in Lck (Gln 423 in c-Src) lies in the activation loop and is poised to sense charged residues downstream of the substrate tyrosine.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of Src-family kinase sequences and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In a 500 ns molecular dynamics simulation of Lck bound to a preferred substrate derived from an ITAM motif, Glu 398 repeatedly forms ion pairs with an arginine residue downstream of the ITAM tyrosine.
source: In a 500 ns molecular dynamics simulation of Lck bound to a preferred substrate derived from an ITAM motif, Glu 398 repeatedly forms ion pairs with an arginine residue downstream of the ITAM tyrosine (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Negatively charged substrate residues in the vicinity of Glu 398 would presumably weaken binding to the Lck activation loop, but not to that of c-Src.
source: Negatively charged substrate residues in this vicinity would presumably weaken binding to the Lck activation loop, but not to that of c-Src, and positively charged residues should be preferred by Lck.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Positively charged residues downstream of the substrate tyrosine should be preferred by Lck.
source: Negatively charged substrate residues in this vicinity would presumably weaken binding to the Lck activation loop, but not to that of c-Src, and positively charged residues should be preferred by Lck.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In c-Src, Arg 472 (Pro 447 in Lck) on the G-helix may assist in the coordination of substrates with negative charge located after the tyrosine.
source: In c-Src, a proximal residue on the G-helix, Arg 472 (Pro 447 in Lck), may assist in the coordination of substrates with negative charge located after the tyrosine (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Asp 463 in Lck (Pro 488 in c-Src) is unlikely to make direct contact with substrates.
source: The third residue of interest, Asp 463 in Lck (Pro 488 in c-Src), is unlikely to make direct contact with substrates.
evidence: This claim is based on the structural analysis.

claim: In simulations of Lck, Asp 463 neutralizes an arginine residue on the F-G loop, which is unpaired in crystal structures of c-Src.
source: In simulations of Lck, Asp 463 neutralizes an arginine residue on the F-G loop, which is unpaired in crystal structures of c-Src (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The F-G loop of tyrosine kinases can control electrostatic selectivity upstream of tyrosine residues in substrates.
source: The F-G loop of tyrosine kinases can control electrostatic selectivity upstream of tyrosine residues in substrates (Shah et al., 2016), and this unpaired arginine in Src-A kinases may explain the slight preference exhibited by c-Src, relative to Lck, for negative charge upstream of the tyrosine.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2016.

claim: The unpaired arginine in Src-A kinases may explain the slight preference exhibited by c-Src, relative to Lck, for negative charge upstream of the tyrosine.
source: The F-G loop of tyrosine kinases can control electrostatic selectivity upstream of tyrosine residues in substrates (Shah et al., 2016), and this unpaired arginine in Src-A kinases may explain the slight preference exhibited by c-Src, relative to Lck, for negative charge upstream of the tyrosine.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis and previous work.

claim: Enrichment scores from screens with c-Src Q423E, R472P, and P488E mutants correlated strongly with those from the wild-type c-Src screen.
source: Enrichment scores from these screens correlated strongly with those from the wild-type c-Src screen, with few substrates being selectively phosphorylated by either wild-type c-Src or a mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Each c-Src mutant (Q423E, R472P, P488E) efficiently phosphorylated ~50 peptides that were not efficiently phosphorylated by wild-type c-Src.
source: Each mutant efficiently phosphorylated ~50 peptides that were not efficiently phosphorylated by wild-type c-Src.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the screening data for the c-Src mutants.

claim: Peptides that were selectively phosphorylated by the c-Src Q423E and R472P mutants, but not wild-type c-Src, showed a clear enrichment in sequences with positive charge downstream of the tyrosine.
source: Analysis of peptides that were selectively phosphorylated by the c-Src Q423E and R472P mutants, but not wild-type c-Src, showed a clear enrichment in sequences with positive charge downstream of the tyrosine (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The c-Src P488E mutant showed a similar, albeit less clear, preference for sequences with positive charge downstream of the tyrosine.
source: The c-Src P488E mutant showed a similar, albeit less clear, preference (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Q423E mutant c-Src gained substantial activity relative to wild-type c-Src toward an Lck-preferred substrate (peptide 2) that contains several positively charged residues downstream of the tyrosine.
source: The Q423E mutant c-Src gained substantial activity relative to wild-type c-Src toward an Lck-preferred substrate (peptide 2) that contains several positively charged residues downstream of the tyrosine, consistent with our structural model.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from in vitro kinetic measurements.

claim: The R472P mutant c-Src had reduced activity against all five peptides tested.
source: The R472P mutant c-Src mutant had reduced activity against all five peptides tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 4); however, this mutant preferentially lost activity against the negatively-charged c-Src-preferred peptides (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The R472P mutant c-Src preferentially lost activity against the negatively-charged c-Src-preferred peptides.
source: The R472P mutant c-Src mutant had reduced activity against all five peptides tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 4); however, this mutant preferentially lost activity against the negatively-charged c-Src-preferred peptides (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The P488E c-Src mutant displayed activity similar to wild-type c-Src against the five substrates tested.
source: The P488E c-Src mutant displayed activity similar to wild-type c-Src against these five substrates, suggesting that this residue may not play a strong role in differentiating the specificities of c-Src and Lck.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from in vitro kinetic measurements.

claim: Residue 488 may not play a strong role in differentiating the specificities of c-Src and Lck.
source: The P488E c-Src mutant displayed activity similar to wild-type c-Src against these five substrates, suggesting that this residue may not play a strong role in differentiating the specificities of c-Src and Lck.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data from in vitro kinetic measurements.

claim: Fyn had intermediate specificity between c-Src and Lck when analyzed with the panel of five purified peptides.
source: We found that Fyn had intermediate specificity between c-Src and Lck when analyzed with the panel of five purified peptides described above (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The Src-B kinase Hck showed the expected Lck-like specificity using the same peptides.
source: The Src-B kinase Hck showed the expected Lck-like specificity using the same peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from in vitro kinetic measurements.

claim: The unexpected divergence between the Src-A kinases c-Src and Fyn may reflect yet unknown selective pressures on the substrate specificity of Fyn.
source: The unexpected divergence between the Src-A kinases c-Src and Fyn may reflect yet unknown selective pressures on the substrate specificity of Fyn.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the observed specificity differences.

claim: Lck and c-Src not only differ in their preference for charged residues, but they also have slightly different preferences at the −1 and +3 positions on substrates.
source: For example, in comparing c-Src and Lck, it is evident that these kinases not only differ in their preference for charged residues, but they also have slightly different preferences at the −1 and +3 positions on substrates (Figures 3B and 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3B and 5A.

claim: Tyrosine kinases are generally most selective with respect to the −1 and +3 substrate positions.
source: Tyrosine kinases are generally most selective with respect to these substrate positions, and many kinases have distinct preferences at these positions (Figure 5A and [Songyang et al., 1995]).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Songyang et al., 1995.

claim: A residue on the F-G loop that lines the catalytic cleft makes direct contacts with −1 residues in both Lck and ZAP-70 simulations.
source: A residue on the F-G loop that lines the catalytic cleft makes direct contacts with −1 residues in both Lck and ZAP-70 simulations (Figure 5B and [Shah et al., 2016]).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Shah et al., 2016.

claim: The F-G loop residue is an isoleucine in Lck and valine in c-Src, consistent with their strong but slightly different preferences for hydrophobic −1 residues.
source: This F-G loop residue is an isoleucine in Lck and valine in c-Src, consistent with their strong but slightly different preferences for hydrophobic −1 residues (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and the structural analysis.

claim: c-Abl has a serine residue at the F-G loop position, which may explain its slightly broadened −1 residue tolerance.
source: c-Abl has a serine residue at this position, which may explain its slightly broadened −1 residue tolerance, and ZAP-70 has a lysine residue, consistent with a strong preference of this kinase for a −1 aspartate or glutamate residue (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis and data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ZAP-70 has a lysine residue at the F-G loop position, consistent with a strong preference of this kinase for a −1 aspartate or glutamate residue.
source: c-Abl has a serine residue at this position, which may explain its slightly broadened −1 residue tolerance, and ZAP-70 has a lysine residue, consistent with a strong preference of this kinase for a −1 aspartate or glutamate residue (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and the structural analysis.

claim: Mutation of the F-G loop residue in c-Src alters −1 residue preferences in accordance with the observations from the structural analysis.
source: Mutation of this F-G loop residue in c-Src alters −1 residue preferences in accordance with these observations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Specific residues in the +3 pocket differentiate the four kinases (Lck, c-Src, c-Abl, ZAP-70).
source: Our simulations, and previous reports (Till et al., 1999), have also identified specific residues in the +3 pocket that differentiate the four kinases described here (Figure 5B); however, the precise rules defining +3 residue preferences are not clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Till et al., 1999.

claim: The precise rules defining +3 residue preferences are not clear.
source: Our simulations, and previous reports (Till et al., 1999), have also identified specific residues in the +3 pocket that differentiate the four kinases described here (Figure 5B); however, the precise rules defining +3 residue preferences are not clear.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current understanding.

claim: Analysis of discrete sequences allows for the identification of independent linear motifs that are buried in the phospho-pLogo diagrams.
source: For example, analysis of discrete sequences allows for the identification of independent linear motifs that are buried in the phospho-pLogo diagrams, and to assess the interdependence of specific residue preferences (Kettenbach et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kettenbach et al., 2012.

claim: Analysis using Motif-X reproduced the known specificity determinants for all four kinases (c-Src, Lck, c-Abl, ZAP-70), primarily at the −3, –1, +1, and +3 positions.
source: This analysis reproduced the known specificity determinants for all four kinases, primarily at the −3, –1, +1, and +3 positions (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: All of the statistically significant independent motifs for the four kinases were defined by single position preferences, suggesting negligible interdependence between favorable sequence features at these positions.
source: Interestingly, all of the statistically significant independent motifs for these four kinases were defined by single position preferences, suggesting negligible interdependence between favorable sequence features at these positions.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis using Motif-X.

claim: The analysis using Motif-X cannot describe conditional negative selection.
source: It is noteworthy, however, that the analysis using Motif-X cannot describe conditional negative selection.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the Motif-X analysis.

claim: It is possible that the presence of a specific amino acid residue at one site may make certain residues unfavorable at another site.
source: It is possible that the presence of a specific amino acid residue at one site may make certain residues unfavorable at another site.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential interdependence of residue preferences.

claim: For each kinase (c-Src, Lck, c-Abl, ZAP-70), only 40–60% of the reported phosphosites in the curated PhosphoSitePlus list were efficiently phosphorylated in the bacterial surface-display setting.
source: For each kinase, only 40–60% of the reported phosphosites in the curated PhosphoSitePlus list were efficiently phosphorylated in the bacterial surface-display setting (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The bacterial surface-display screens faithfully recapitulate phosphorylation efficiencies measured with purified peptides and kinases.
source: The bacterial surface-display screens faithfully recapitulate phosphorylation efficiencies measured with purified peptides and kinases (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2016.

claim: The inability of the screens to fully recapitulate reported biologically relevant kinase-substrate interactions can be explained by inaccuracies in databases of kinase-substrate pairs.
source: The inability of these screens to fully recapitulate reported biologically relevant kinase-substrate interactions can be explained in at least three ways. (1) Few databases of kinase-substrate pairs are completely accurate, as it remains challenging to unambiguously determine in vivo substrates of protein kinases.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the discrepancy between the screening data and the PhosphoSitePlus database.

claim: Substrate selection in vivo is not only driven by primary sequence recognition in the kinase active site, but also by interactions outside of the active site that dictate sub-cellular localization.
source: (2) Substrate selection in vivo is not only driven by primary sequence recognition in the kinase active site, but also by interactions outside of the active site that dictate sub-cellular localization.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the discrepancy between the screening data and the PhosphoSitePlus database.

claim: Natural substrates of kinases are not necessarily optimized for maximal phosphorylation efficiency.
source: (3) Natural substrates of kinases are not necessarily optimized for maximal phosphorylation efficiency.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the discrepancy between the screening data and the PhosphoSitePlus database.

claim: Sequence recognition by tyrosine kinase domains can play an important role in shaping signaling pathways.
source: Despite the observed discrepancies between our screens and a database of biologically-relevant interactions, the data presented here, and in our previous manuscript (Shah et al., 2016), support the notion that sequence recognition by tyrosine kinase domains can play an important role in shaping signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on the data presented in this study and the authors' previous work.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the substrate preferences and evolutionary relationships of kinases: closely related kinases typically have similar sequence preferences.
source: There is a strong correlation between the substrate preferences and evolutionary relationships of kinases: closely related kinases typically have similar sequence preferences (Songyang et al., 1995; Deng et al., 2014; Schmitz et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Songyang et al., 1995; Deng et al., 2014; Schmitz et al., 1996.

claim: Differences in specificity between the Src-family kinases have been observed previously, using surface-plasmon resonance detection of phosphorylation in a broad range of potential substrates.
source: Differences in specificity between the Src-family kinases have been observed previously, using surface-plasmon resonance detection of phosphorylation in a broad range of potential substrates, although a clear picture of the structural differences underlying the observed specificity differences did not emerge from that study (Takeda et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takeda et al., 2010.

claim: There is a subtle divergence in substrate specificities within the Src-family kinases, whereby Lck disfavors the phosphorylation of negatively charged substrates relative to c-Src.
source: We now show that there is a subtle divergence in substrate specificities within the Src-family kinases, whereby Lck disfavors the phosphorylation of negatively charged substrates relative to c-Src.
evidence: This claim is based on the data presented in this study.

claim: The electrostatic preference of Lck reflects a branch-point in the evolution of Src-family kinases, with the Src-B lineage specialized to act in immune cells in coordination with Syk-family kinases, and the Src-A lineage acting broadly across a variety of cell types.
source: Our analyses suggest that this electrostatic preference reflects a branch-point in the evolution of Src-family kinases, with the Src-B lineage specialized to act in immune cells in coordination with Syk-family kinases, and the Src-A lineage acting broadly across a variety of cell types.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the data presented in this study.

claim: The substrate-recognition properties of closely related kinase domains can be altered subtly over the course of evolution to refine specificity in response to specific functional requirements.
source: More generally, our results demonstrate how the substrate-recognition properties of closely related kinase domains can be altered subtly over the course of evolution to refine specificity in response to specific functional requirements.
evidence: This claim is a general conclusion based on the data presented in this study.

claim: The high-throughput method to interrogate the Human-pTyr library can be applied to the analysis of the specificity of any tyrosine kinase and is easy to deploy.
source: The high-throughput method to interrogate this library can be applied to the analysis of the specificity of any tyrosine kinase and is easy to deploy.
evidence: This claim is based on the methodology developed in this study.

claim: The power of the high-throughput method derives from the increased speed and accuracy of modern sequencing methods.
source: The power of the method derives from the increased speed and accuracy of modern sequencing methods.
evidence: This claim is based on the methodology developed in this study.

claim: The approach will aid in the identification of unknown tyrosine kinase-substrate interactions in phosphotyrosine signaling pathways.
source: We envision that our approach will not only guide our understanding of sequence recognition by tyrosine kinase domains, as described in this study, but also aid in the identification of unknown tyrosine kinase-substrate interactions in phosphotyrosine signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the future applications of the method.
